components.text: Whether the stated prebiotic sequence supplies chemically feasible transitions to replication and cellular organization.
Whether the proposed sequence supplies chemically viable transitions to self-replication and cellular enclosure.
Whether replicator-first, metabolism-first, and membrane-first approaches avoid their distinct chemical obstacles.
Whether naturalistic background commitments legitimately govern assessment of cellular evidence or prejudge the agency question.
Whether prior commitment to natural-law explanations improperly forecloses an agency inference from cellular evidence.
Whether allowing design language while excluding investigable intervention leaves science unable to assess agency.
Whether methodological naturalism is an arbitrary exclusion of agency or has independent pragmatic justification.
Whether methodological naturalism has non-question-begging warrant despite constraining scientific explanations to natural causes.
Whether acknowledging the method as philosophical makes it arbitrary or empirically impotent.
Whether identified chemical obstacles invalidate natural origin pathways or instead coexist with cumulative experimental progress.
Whether present incompleteness establishes natural insufficiency and an affirmative requirement for intelligent agency.
Whether concrete experimental progress leaves the natural prebiotic program evidentially viable despite unresolved transitions.
Whether fatty-acid vesicles and alternative precursor chemistry contact the alleged membrane and polymer obstacles.
Whether acknowledged gaps amount to evidence that natural processes are insufficient.
Whether an agency account can qualify as scientific despite naturalism's pragmatic history and the account's scriptural inspiration.
Whether background commitments should exclude an agency model before its predictions are empirically tested.
Whether an agency or creation model can qualify as scientific by generating predictions and guiding empirical research.
Whether a hypothesis's scriptural inspiration disqualifies it independently of its testable empirical consequences.
Whether biological dysfunction is unexpected under intelligent design and therefore favors wholly unbroken natural development.
Whether biological dysfunction is incompatible with intelligent design or can arise after creation under natural laws.
Whether local suboptimality can result from optimization tradeoffs at the whole-system level.
Whether lawful natural processes and intelligent creation are exclusive alternatives or can occupy different causal roles.
Whether the operation of unbroken laws rules out discrete intelligent intervention in the history of life.
Whether lawful natural processes and discrete intelligent intervention must be treated as mutually exclusive causal options.
Whether regular natural law can operate after an intervention without excluding the proposed intervention itself.
Whether biological information must be explained as an independently supplied, artifact-like product of intelligent agency.
Whether the production of organized biological outcomes necessarily requires foresight or investigator-like agency.
Whether biological information requires an independently supplied intelligent source rather than cumulative selection.
Whether information accumulation supplies a positive reason to require intelligent agency.
Whether coordinated cellular function requires the full modern minimum at once or can arise through selectable proto-systems.
Whether coordinated molecular function requires foresight analogous to human engineering.
Whether coordinated cellular function must appear at modern minimum complexity rather than through selectable intermediates.
Whether molecular cooperation requires foresight instead of differential survival of workable arrangements.
Whether proto-ribosomal intermediates provide an incremental route toward coordinated cellular machinery.
Whether unresolved prebiotic obstacles can presently be overcome by appealing to possible undiscovered catalysts or future research.
Whether a proposed sequence is presently sufficient without catalysts capable of the required transformations.
Whether possible future catalytic discoveries can presently warrant confidence in a complete natural prebiotic pathway.
Whether known limitations on catalytic range undermine the asserted transition from prebiotic compounds to replicators.
